title: Connection Pooling and Exhaustion
description: Understand how ADO.NET connection pooling works, why pools exhaust in production, and how to diagnose and prevent connection pool exhaustion.

data.text: Opening a new TCP connection to SQL Server is expensive. It involves authentication, TLS negotiation, and session establishment. To avoid paying this cost on every query, ADO.NET (and most database drivers) use **connection pooling**: they keep a set of open, idle connections ready for reuse. When your application calls `SqlConnection.Open()`, the driver checks the pool first. If an idle connection exists, it hands it to you instantly.

Connection pooling is automatic and invisible — until it runs out. When the pool is exhausted and every connection is in use, `SqlConnection.Open()` waits for a connection to return to the pool or throws a timeout error. In production, pool exhaustion is one of the most common causes of 'the database is slow' complaints that are actually application-side problems.

ADO.NET creates a separate pool for every unique connection string. A pool is identified by the exact connection string (including whitespace). When you call `SqlConnection.Close()` or `Dispose()`, the physical connection is not closed — it is returned to the pool. The pool then keeps it open, ready for the next `Open()` call from the same connection string.

data.caption: The lifecycle of a pooled connection: open, use, close (return to pool), and reuse.
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    App[Application calls Open()] --> Pool{Idle connection in pool?}
    Pool -->|Yes| Reuse[Reuse existing connection]
    Pool -->|No| Create[Create new connection]
    Create --> Max{At max pool size?}
    Max -->|Yes| Wait[Wait for return]
    Max -->|No| New[Open new physical connection]
    New --> Use[Application uses connection]
    Reuse --> Use
    Use --> Close[Application calls Close()]
    Close --> Return[Return connection to pool]
    Return --> Pool

data.text: Pool exhaustion typically manifests as timeout errors or 'Timeout expired' exceptions, often during peak traffic. Because the timeout happens in the application before a query even reaches SQL Server, developers sometimes misdiagnose it as a database problem. The database may be perfectly healthy while the application cannot get a connection.

data.title: Symptoms of Pool Exhaustion
items: SqlException: 'Timeout expired. The timeout period elapsed prior to obtaining a connection from the pool.'
High CPU on the application server (threads waiting for connections spin and consume CPU)
No corresponding spike in SQL Server activity — the database is idle while the app is failing
Errors appear suddenly under load, then disappear when traffic drops
Connection pool performance counters show zero available connections

data.text: The fastest way to confirm pool exhaustion is to use .NET performance counters. The '.NET Data Provider for SqlServer' category exposes counters for the number of connections in the pool, the number of active connections, and the number of connection requests that had to wait. If 'NumberOfPooledConnections' is at the max and 'NumberOfActiveConnections' equals it, the pool is exhausted.

data.title: Monitor Connection Pool Performance Counters
data.content: Use PowerShell to read .NET connection pool counters in real time.
data.code:
Get-Counter -Counter '\.NET Data Provider for SqlServer\NumberOfPooledConnections',
                  '\.NET Data Provider for SqlServer\NumberOfActiveConnections',
                  '\.NET Data Provider for SqlServer\NumberOfNonPooledConnections',
                  '\.NET Data Provider for SqlServer\NumberOfFreeConnections',
                  '\.NET Data Provider for SqlServer\NumberOfActiveConnectionPools'

data.title: Max Pool Size Defaults to 100
data.text: The default max pool size is 100 connections per connection string per AppDomain. A web farm with 20 servers can open 2,000 connections to SQL Server. If your database has a lower connection limit or your SQL Server is configured for fewer worker threads, you will hit resource limits long before pools exhaust.

Pool exhaustion is almost always caused by application code that holds connections open longer than necessary. The most common culprit is opening a connection, performing a small query, and then holding the connection open while processing business logic, rendering a page, or waiting for an external API.

data.title: Connection Pool Best Practices
items: Open connections as late as possible and close them as early as possible — use `using` statements to guarantee disposal
Never hold a connection open during business logic, user input waits, or external API calls
Use async/await with `OpenAsync()` to avoid blocking threads while waiting for a connection
Keep connection strings identical across the application — even a whitespace difference creates a separate pool
Set `Max Pool Size` explicitly in production based on load testing, not defaults
Monitor pool counters in production and alert when available connections drop below a threshold

data.title: The Using Statement Is Non-Negotiable
data.text: In C#, always wrap `SqlConnection`, `SqlCommand`, and `SqlDataReader` in `using` statements. This guarantees the connection is returned to the pool even if an exception occurs. A single forgotten connection in a high-traffic path can exhaust the entire pool.

items.question: Should I increase Max Pool Size to fix exhaustion?
items.answer: Increasing Max Pool Size is rarely the right fix. It masks the real problem — connections being held too long. A larger pool puts more load on SQL Server (more worker threads, more memory) and delays the point at which you notice the leak. Fix the code first.

items.question: Does connection pooling work with Entity Framework?
items.answer: Yes. Entity Framework Core uses ADO.NET connection pooling under the hood. The same rules apply: DbContext instances should be short-lived, and you should never hold a DbContext open across an HTTP request boundary.

items.question: What causes 'The connection was not closed' errors?
items.answer: This error typically means a connection was not returned to the pool — it was left open, leaked, or the application domain recycled while connections were active. Check for missing Dispose() calls or unhandled exceptions that skip the using block.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Connection pooling reuses physical TCP connections to reduce overhead — pools are keyed by exact connection string
Pool exhaustion causes timeout exceptions in the application, not in SQL Server — the database may be idle while the app fails
Diagnose with .NET performance counters: if pooled equals active and free equals zero, the pool is exhausted
The fix is almost always in the application: open late, close early, use using statements, and never hold connections during business logic
Max Pool Size is a ceiling, not a target — design for the smallest pool that handles peak load comfortably
data.takeaway: Connection pooling is a performance feature, not a capacity plan. Treat connection lifetime as a critical resource: the shorter the lifetime, the healthier the pool.
